name: Quichua, Imbabura Highland
catalog_quote: Stress is indicated by a combination of loudness and high pitch. Stress in Imbabura Quechua is non-distinctive. It falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. (Cole 1982:208) || Intonational accent is on P of phrase. If used contrastively it is on P of the contrasted word. Accent not only shows higher pitch, but also lengthening. (Cole 1982:210) || Cole (1982:208) states that IK carries stress…

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (penultimate rule unchanged; drop from the strict set or at minimum fill exst/caution): the held deciding source itself (Gualapuro 2017 sect. 7.2.2 pp.44-45) lists morpheme-conditioned antepenult (validator -mi ['wa.si.mi], progressive -hun [mi'ku.na.huN]), final (dubitative -cha [kal.pan.ga.'tSa]) and stem-retained stress under emphatic -yari, and Adelaar & Muysken 2004:206 (via held LOT188 p.~190) note 'few instances of last-syllable stress'. If Cole 1982:208-210 shows these are enclitic/phrase-level emphatic effects outside the word domain, strict can be retained with a caution note instead.

sources.quote: "The usual pattern of stress in Quichua is to accent the next-to-last syllable of the word. This is like Spanish." (1-C p.45); "When -rka is added, the accent shifts one syllable to the right: mikuni --> mikurkani. This keeps the stress on the next to last syllable of the word." (2-E p.74). (The held Part 1, ED058782, has no stress statement — pronunciation is deferred to Part 2.)
